readerTitle: The steel shop that promised 10 days and took 17
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (맞춤 철제 선반 제작·배송 공방, 온라인 주문) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 주문이 늦어질 때는 모두를 더 일하게 하기 전에 주문 하나를 끝까지 따라가 가장 느린 단계를 찾고, 그 단계를 지키고, 그 단계의 시간을 갉아먹는 실수를 처음부터 막는다.
misconception: 주문이 밀리면 사람을 더 쓰거나 모두 더 빨리, 더 오래 일하면 해결된다.

sources.text: Goldratt, E. M. & Cox, J. (1984). The Goal. 병목(제약) 관리의 고전적 설명
운영관리의 표준 개념 (프로세스 맵, 병목, 용량, 표준화, 원천 품질, 지속적 개선)
모든 수치와 회사는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 리드타임 계산: 실제 작업 약 4일(절단 1 + 용접 1 + 도장 1 + 포장 1) + 대기 13일 = 17일. 이후 12일 → 9일로 줄어드는 흐름이 카드 3~6 사이에서 일관되는지 확인하세요.
재작업 비율: 처음 10건 중 1건(10%), 개선 후 50건 중 1건(2%). 성수기 수요 증가 30%는 가정입니다. 카드 간 숫자가 서로 맞는지 다시 확인하세요.
"병목이 개선되면 다른 단계로 옮겨간다"는 제약이론의 일반 원리로 서술했습니다. 특정 연구 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The steel shop that promised 10 days and took 17
body: You run a 12-person workshop that makes custom steel shelving. Customers design their units online, and you ship them by freight. Your website promises delivery in 10 days.
Lately the average is 17. Complaints are up, and two business customers have quietly stopped ordering. Your team already feels busy. Over the next few cards, you make the calls.

image.label: Workshop with a calendar showing late orders
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 철제 가공 공방 내부, 벽에 걸린 달력에 빨간 표시가 여러 개, 출고 대기 중인 상자들. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Orders are late. What's your first move?
body: Every station looks busy. Your team leads each have a different theory about the problem.

options.text: Add a Saturday shift for the whole team
options.feedback: You get more hours, but you pay overtime at every station. If one step is holding things up, most of the extra work just piles up in front of it.

options.text: Follow five recent orders from click to truck, timing each step and each wait
options.feedback: It costs a few days of watching, not money. You trade a quick fix for a clear picture of where the time actually goes.

options.text: Replace the old laser cutter with a faster one
options.feedback: A big spend based on a guess. If cutting isn't the slow step, finished parts will just reach the real problem sooner.

cards.title: The pile in front of the oven
body: Say you chose to follow the orders. Hands-on work takes about 4 days. The other 13 are waiting, mostly in a pile of welded parts outside the powder-coating oven. The oven sits empty during lunch and while parts are hung on racks.
**The whole shop can only ship as fast as the oven.** What now?

image.label: Process flow with a big pile before one step
image.brief: 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 흐르는 공정도: Cut → Weld → Coat → Pack → Truck. Coat 앞에만 부품 상자가 높이 쌓여 있고 나머지 단계 앞은 비어 있음.

options.text: Speed up cutting and welding so coating gets parts sooner
options.feedback: The pile in front of the oven just grows. You'd add effort where it changes nothing.

options.text: Keep the oven running nonstop: welders pre-hang parts on racks, and lunch breaks are staggered
options.feedback: Every hour the oven runs is an hour the whole shop gains. It costs some shuffling of jobs, not new equipment.
Right place, but a big cost. The oven you have still sits idle part of the day.

cards.softwareNote: In a software team, the oven is often code review or the one person who approves releases. Finished work waits there, and writing code faster only makes the queue longer.

cards.title: Some orders go through the oven twice.
body: Say you kept the oven running. Delivery drops to about 12 days. But about 1 in 10 orders comes back for recoating: wrong color, or a size misread from a customer's note. Each redo uses the very oven time you just freed up.

options.text: Add a final inspection before packing
options.feedback: Fewer bad units reach customers. But the mistake is found after it has already used cutting, welding and oven time.

options.text: Make the online form use fixed size and color options, and check each order once before cutting
options.feedback: Errors are stopped where they start, before they touch the slowest step. Customers lose a little freedom in how they describe orders.

options.text: Ask everyone to read orders more carefully
options.feedback: Free, and it feels responsible. But the same unclear notes keep arriving, so the same mistakes return.

cards.title: Busy season is coming.
body: Say you fixed the order form. Redos fall to about 1 in 50, and delivery is near 9 days. Next quarter, you expect about 30% more orders.

options.text: Call it solved and move on to sales
options.feedback: You save management time now. But nobody will notice when the pile starts growing again.

options.text: Check whether the oven can handle 30% more, then hold a 15-minute weekly review of delivery time, pile size and redos
options.feedback: A small, steady habit that catches problems while they're cheap. It costs a quarter hour a week.

options.text: Hire two more welders for the season
options.feedback: You'd pay for more welded parts that can't get through the oven any faster.

cards.title: Same team, same building, faster orders.
body: No new hires and no new machines. Each step came from seeing where orders actually waited.

breakdown.label: Oven kept running
breakdown.detail: The slowest step stopped sitting idle

breakdown.label: Redos
breakdown.detail: Down from 1 in 10 after the form fix

cards.title: The slowest step moves.
body: Once the oven speeds up, packing or freight pickup may become the new bottleneck. That's why the weekly review matters more than any single fix.
Also, letting welders sit idle sometimes is fine. Busy stations everywhere aren't the goal; finished orders are.
And five orders is a small sample. Treat the first map as a starting guess, then keep checking.

cards.title: Follow the order, find the slowest step, then protect it.
body: Each call you made maps to an idea from this unit:
list: **Follow five orders:** see the process before fixing it
**Keep the oven running:** bottlenecks and capacity
**Fix the order form:** standardization and quality at the source
cards.callout: **Try it today:** follow one order from start to finish. Write down how long it is worked on, and how long it waits.
